articles.originalTitle: Matteo Thun designs Torre Velasca interiors using “the building itself as the starting point” - Dezeen
articles.title: Matteo Thun Designs New Interiors for Historic Torre Velasca in Milan
articles.excerpt: Italian architect Matteo Thun has redesigned the interiors of seventy-two flats on the upper floors of Milan's iconic Torre Velasca skyscraper, drawing inspiration from the building's original materials and colours.
articles.content: Italian architect Matteo Thun based his interior design for 72 flats on the upper floors of Milan's iconic Torre Velasca tower on the building's original materials and colours. The suites and duplex penthouses within the skyscraper, built in the 1950s by the BBPR studio, were approached with a focus on reinterpretation. The design team preserved original details including doors, window frames, loggias, and tiles in bathrooms and kitchens. These elements were juxtaposed with custom modern furniture and design references spanning the 1950s to the 1980s. The colour palette was derived directly from the pink plaster on Torre Velasca's facade and the blue and green floor tiles found in the loggias. Living rooms feature pale pink wall coverings that resemble the building's facade, while darker shades of green and blue define entrance areas and bedrooms. In addition to the apartments, Thun designed the reception, lobby, and ground-floor corridors, describing the undertaking as an architectural lesson for his studio.

articles.originalTitle: How Going Blind Made Doris Salcedo’s Art Bigger and Better - ARTnews.com
articles.title: How Losing Vision Shifted Doris Salcedo Toward Large-Scale Collaboration
articles.excerpt: Diagnosed with a rare genetic eye condition that left her legally blind, Colombian artist Doris Salcedo has shifted from solo improvisation to large-scale collaborative works created with assistants.
articles.content: Diagnosed with Stargardt disease at age 31, Colombian artist Doris Salcedo gradually lost her central vision and is now legally blind. While she initially mourned the loss of independent studio improvisation, this transition led her to work closely with assistants and collaborators, including architect Carlos Granada. Her upcoming exhibition at White Cube Gallery in New York features a nearly 30-foot-tall house woven entirely from human hair, a painstaking collaborative process that took dozens of assistants three years to complete. Salcedo notes that such monumental works would be impossible to accomplish alone. Known for monumental anti-monuments such as Fragmentos—which incorporated melted weapons from the FARC guerrilla group to commemorate a Colombian peace agreement—Salcedo's recent works address global housing crises and forced displacement, specifically focusing on the deliberate destruction of homes in conflict zones such as Ukraine, Gaza, Syria, and Sudan. By transforming delicate human hair into sturdy structural forms, her work aims to reflect both the vulnerability and resilience of displaced populations.

articles.originalTitle: Berkshire Glade by Turkel Design - Architectural Record
articles.title: Berkshire Glade Multi-Generational Residence Completed in Massachusetts
articles.excerpt: Located in the Berkshire hills of Massachusetts, Berkshire Glade was designed by Turkel Design as a multigenerational vacation home and future residence. Completed in May 2025, the 6,510-square-foot project comprises a primary residence and a guest house.
articles.content: Situated in the Berkshire hills of western Massachusetts, the Berkshire Glade project was designed as a multigenerational vacation home and future permanent residence for a couple with careers in New York and Boston. Spanning 6,510 square feet, the structure designed by Turkel Design overlooks a wooded hillside and Mount Washington. The design links two distinct volumes, a primary residence and a guest house, through a covered porch anchored by a fireplace. This layout balances shared family gatherings with individual privacy. The engineered wood structure relies on Douglas fir glue-laminated beams and thermally modified hemlock. The exterior is clad in Japanese charred wood known as shou sugi ban, which offers resistance to rot and insects. Wall systems, roofing, flooring, windows, doors, and custom cabinetry were fabricated as a package in a climate-controlled facility and shipped to the site for precision assembly. Built on a 120-acre site, the project reached completion in May 2025.

articles.originalTitle: Edgar Degas | Promenade beside the Sea | L819 - The National Gallery, London
articles.title: Edgar Degas's Early Work Promenade beside the Sea on Display in London
articles.excerpt: Held in the collection of The National Gallery, Edgar Degas's oil sketch Promenade beside the Sea, painted around 1860, reflects the artist's early explorations of equine movement.
articles.content: Promenade beside the Sea by Edgar Degas, on display at The National Gallery, is an early oil sketch created around 1860, shortly after the artist established his first studio in Paris. The artwork depicts an elegantly attired couple on horseback riding along the coast at sunset. The gentleman wears black and a top hat, while the lady sits side-saddle in a dark riding habit, set in the Bay of Naples, an area Degas visited on multiple occasions. The theme of horse and rider is a recurrent subject through which Degas explored movement and motion. The artist suggests the gait of the horses using open brushwork. Although giving the impression of an outdoor study, the work was likely produced in the studio using earlier preparatory sketches. Measuring 22.5 by 32.5 cm and executed in oil on canvas, the piece is part of the Gere Collection on long-term loan to The National Gallery.

articles.originalTitle: Rome’s Galleria Borghese’s $11.15 M. Extension Is Moving Forward Despite Pushback - ARTnews.com
articles.title: Rome's Galleria Borghese Moves Forward With $11.15 Million Extension Despite Strong Backlash
articles.excerpt: Rome's 17th-century Galleria Borghese museum is advancing an 11.15 million dollar extension project to address tourist influx, drawing sharp criticism and pushback from heritage groups and politicians alike.
articles.content: Rome's 17th-century museum Galleria Borghese has launched an architectural competition for a 3,000-square-meter extension to address an influx of 700,000 annual visitors. Museum director Francesca Cappelletti noted that despite a daily cap of 2,000 visitors and online booking requirements, international groups daily find themselves unable to enter. Supported by Rome's Ministry of Cultural Heritage and the municipality, the project is estimated to cost 11.15 million dollars. It aims to exhibit stored works, host exhibitions, and open a restaurant, bookstore, and laboratory. Cappelletti stated that the solution must involve a contemporary structure without altering existing heritage. The competition is organized by engineering firm Proger Spa, with an independent jury selecting the winner in May 2027. However, the plan has encountered severe backlash. Alix van Buren, president of the Friends of the Villa Borghese association, called the proposal a grotesque blasphemy. Michele Campisi of heritage group Italia Nostra termed the plans bizarre, while art history professor Tomaso Montanari described the extension as moronic. Fabio Rampelli, vice-president of Italy's lower house of parliament, publicly called for Cappelletti's resignation over the controversial proposal.

articles.originalTitle: Italian design moguls to launch Fondazione Vezza public art project in Piedmont next September - The Art Newspaper
articles.title: New Public Art Project to Launch Among Monastery Ruins in Piedmont
articles.excerpt: Entrepreneurs Sandra and Charley Vezza are establishing a contemporary art trail in woodland around monastery ruins in Monforte d'Alba, northern Italy.
articles.content: Italian entrepreneurs Sandra Vezza and her son Charley Vezza are establishing a new contemporary art hub in Monforte d'Alba, located in northern Italy's Langhe wine region. The initiative will develop a site-specific public art trail over the next decade through the woodland surrounding the medieval San Pietro monastery ruins. Opening next September, the project will be inaugurated with large-scale installations by US artist Kathleen Ryan and Italian sculptor Alessandro Pessoli. Flavio del Monte, former institutional relations director at Milan's Massimo de Carlo gallery, will oversee the project, which invites artists annually to engage with the site's history and landscape. Funded by Sandra and Charley Vezza with confidential budget costs, the permanently installed artworks will be housed on site for the public with free admission.

articles.originalTitle: powerhouse parramatta's steel-latticed museum opens with art by es devlin and james turrell - Designboom
articles.title: Powerhouse Parramatta Opens New Cultural Institution and Museum Building
articles.excerpt: Designed by Moreau Kusunoki and Genton, Powerhouse Parramatta opens on November 7th, 2026. As New South Wales' largest museum, the facility launches with five inaugural exhibitions featuring installations by Es Devlin and James Turrell.
articles.content: Located along the Parramatta River in Western Sydney, Powerhouse Parramatta officially opens to the public on November 7th, 2026. Designed by architecture studios Moreau Kusunoki and Genton, the cultural building stands as the largest museum ever built in New South Wales. Encompassing over 18,000 square meters of public and exhibition space, the institution brings together collections spanning art, design, science, and technology. More than 3,000 objects are presented across five inaugural exhibitions, including a presentation developed with OMA/AMO. The building features a distinctive white steel structural lattice that enables expansive, column-free interiors. The opening program includes The Turning, a multi-work exhibition by British artist Es Devlin exploring human perception and memory, and Shangri La, a monumental light installation by American artist James Turrell. Alongside the galleries, the project introduces waterfront public spaces, a rooftop garden, and an observatory. The opening initiates a 23-day festival of performances, workshops, and public conversations across the new cultural facilities.

articles.originalTitle: About the Constantinople to Istanbul: One City, Two Empires exhibition - Victoria and Albert Museum
articles.title: V&A Museum Explores Byzantine and Ottoman Legacy in Major Exhibition
articles.excerpt: The Victoria and Albert Museum is hosting Constantinople to Istanbul: One City, Two Empires, an exhibition exploring 1,600 years of artistic production from AD 330 to 1922.
articles.content: V&A South Kensington in London is presenting Constantinople to Istanbul: One City, Two Empires, an exhibition spanning the period from AD 330 to 1922. The exhibition examines the art and design traditions of both the Byzantine and Ottoman empires, highlighting their creative legacy that shaped the Mediterranean and beyond. Spread across four main sections, the exhibition features over 200 objects, including rare decorative arts, fine silks, textiles, ceramic tiles, mosaics, precious metalwork, jewelry, sculpture, architectural furnishings, manuscripts, and paintings. The first section, Roman Beginnings, explores the refounding of the city in AD 330 as the capital of the Roman Empire under Constantine the Great, focusing on its infrastructure and the Hippodrome. Heaven and Earth, the second section, explores how art and architecture served Christianity. Power and Reach examines how the Ottoman court projected authority through visual spectacle and luxury materials, while the final section, Life in the City, investigates the city's cosmopolitan character, religious coexistence, and 19th-century shifts in style. The exhibition remains open until 9 May 2027.

articles.originalTitle: 2028 Whitney Biennial to Be Curated by Meg Onli and Zack Winokur - ARTnews.com
articles.title: Whitney Museum Appoints Meg Onli and Zack Winokur to Curate 2028 Biennial
articles.excerpt: The Whitney Museum has named museum curator Meg Onli and director Zack Winokur as the curators for the upcoming 83rd edition of the Whitney Biennial, opening in March 2028.
articles.content: The Whitney Museum announced the curatorial team for the upcoming 83rd edition of its biennial, scheduled to open in March 2028. Museum curator Meg Onli and director Zack Winokur have been appointed as co-curators for the exhibition. Onli, who previously co-curated the 2024 edition, joined the Whitney as a curator-at-large in 2023. Her background includes serving as co-director and curator of the Underground Museum in Los Angeles, and she is currently co-curating a retrospective for Roy Lichtenstein at the Whitney alongside artist Alex Da Corte. Winokur is the co-founder of the American Modern Opera Company and has directed numerous productions across opera, theater, and dance. Whitney director Scott Rothkopf stated that the partnership between Onli and Winokur promises a radical new vision for the 2028 Biennial. Both curators expressed enthusiasm for fostering experimentation and supporting artists across disciplines as preparations begin for the major exhibition, which follows the conclusion of the 2026 iteration.

articles.originalTitle: Best Government/Public Building: Essex County Wynona Lipman Family Courthouse - Engineering News-Record
articles.title: Essex County Wynona Lipman Family Courthouse Wins Recognition
articles.excerpt: Built in Newark, the 266,000-square-foot, eight-story Essex County Wynona Lipman Family Courthouse consolidates previously dispersed family courts into a central location.
articles.content: Situated in Newark, the 266,000-square-foot, eight-story Essex County Wynona Lipman Family Courthouse consolidates previously dispersed family and children courts, probation services, and domestic violence units into a central urban location. The primary public entry is carved out under the upper floors to form a plaza as an extension of the streetscape. According to the submission, family courts require a de-escalating environment, addressed here by a multicolor art-glass two-story translucent screen on the public street wall and separate child-friendly playrooms in waiting areas. Constructing the massive complex in downtown Newark required meticulous coordination, including working within strict property lines, managing daily traffic flows, and minimizing disruptions to neighbors. The interior design divides spaces to separate hostile parties while accommodating sensitive zones, and integrates modern security with separate private entry points, holding cells, secure sallyports, and underground parking for judges. To counter unpredictable conditions, the project team relied on daily meetings and constant communication, allowing project managers, superintendents, and safety managers to address obstacles, coordinate daily tasks, and adapt in real time alongside cooperation with the city of Newark.

articles.originalTitle: Circularity Cabin by Takaaki Fuji + Yuko Fuji Architecture - Architectural Record
articles.title: Circularity Cabin Designed for Disassembly Completed in Zushi, Japan
articles.excerpt: Designed by Takaaki Fuji and Yuko Fuji Architecture in Zushi, Circularity Cabin was built to be unbolted and relocated due to a planned road widening project. Completed in March 2023, the 642-square-foot home uses bolts and screws without adhesives.
articles.content: Located in a valley in Zushi, south of Tokyo, the Circularity Cabin was designed as a primary residence for a couple and their young child. Because approximately half of the site lies within a planned road widening zone, the building was engineered to be unbolted, stored, and reconstructed elsewhere before its materials wear out, or returned to the timber market. Spanning 642 square feet across two floors, the house designed by Takaaki Fuji and Yuko Fuji Architecture is assembled entirely from stock lumber joined solely with bolts and screws, avoiding adhesives or cut joinery. The structure employs three stock lumber sections. Paired beams stack rather than interlock, allowing a single wrench to free any joint. While the street-facing side features a solid wooden wall, fresh air enters through clerestory windows and descends via a slatted second-floor deck. Built on a 615-square-foot lot, the project had a construction cost of $104,000 and was completed in March 2023.

articles.originalTitle: John Berger In The Pits - ArtReview
articles.title: John Berger and Émile Zola on Miners and Class Struggle
articles.excerpt: An examination of writers and their working-class connections looks at Émile Zola's Germinal and John Berger's 1973 documentary to explore pit conditions and authorial positions.
articles.content: In February 1884, Émile Zola descended into a coalmine in Anzin, Northern France, to conduct research for his 1885 novel Germinal. Frederick Brown, in his 1995 biography of Zola, noted that the writer's stout physique made underground exploration particularly inconvenient. Similarly, English art critic and novelist John Berger descended into a pit in Creswell on the Nottinghamshire-Derbyshire border for his rarely screened 1973 BBC documentary Germinal. Berger, an avowed Marxist, observed in the documentary that the underground air was hot and silted with coal dust, leaving less space for the body. Berger surmised that Zola, despite his working-class sympathies, must have felt self-conscious living as a wealthy and successful author in a villa near Paris. Both writers shared several biographical parallels, including writing for periodicals and maintaining homes in the French countryside. While Zola earned significant royalties from depicting the struggles of the poor in his writing, Berger's engagement with disenfranchised groups followed his Booker Prize-winning novel G. In his televised homage, Berger recited passages from Zola's novel concerning the vengeance of the working class as residents of Creswell went about their daily lives.

articles.originalTitle: Biennale Arte 2026 | Morocco Pavilion: DECLOSION - La Biennale di Venezia
articles.title: Venice Biennale 2026 Morocco Pavilion Announces Declosion Performance
articles.excerpt: Scheduled for the Arsenale during the 2026 Venice Biennale, the Morocco Pavilion will present the performance Declosion, drawing on the cosmology of Hesiod's Theogony.
articles.content: As part of the 2026 Venice Biennale, the Morocco Pavilion at the Arsenale will host the performance titled Declosion. Drawing from the chaos narrative in Hesiod's Theogony, the performance invokes Clotho, the figure who spins the thread of life. Engaging in a dialogue with Amina Agueznay's artwork, the event explores the cyclical rhythm of existence spanning birth, life, and death. Featuring performer Inès Abergel within the installation Asǝṭṭa, the work reveals the transition from emptiness to fullness and nonbeing to being. Artistic support for the performance is provided by Amina Agueznay, with music composition by Guilain Delanoue. Movement advisors include Alice Dardenne and Romane Piffaut, while scenography is advised by Amine Slimani and Federico Urso. Objects for the installation are crafted by Malika Benmoumen, Mahdia Anoufr, Koltoum Gaddem, Khaddouj Alja, and Florian SôngNguyen. The performance is scheduled for November 21, 2026, from 16:30 to 16:50.

articles.originalTitle: making room for nature: the urban landscapes of kongjian yu - Designboom
articles.title: Urban Landscape Projects in China Examine Climate Adaptation and Ecological Transformation
articles.excerpt: A book authored by Harvard professor Charles Waldheim examines sixty landscape architecture experiments realized by Turenscape, documenting how these projects respond to climate change and flooding.
articles.content: In Landscapes for Adaptation: Evidence from China, Harvard professor Charles Waldheim examines sixty built experiments realized in China. The projects executed by Turenscape over the past two decades address how landscape architecture can respond to climate volatility, floods, and ecological change. Turenscape founder Kongjian Yu advocates that urban development should work with natural processes, utilizing water, vegetation, and ecological systems as infrastructure. In Shanghai, Houtan Park transforms an industrially degraded site into an ecological and public space. A constructed wetland within the park uses terraces and aquatic plants to treat river water and support flood management. Similarly, Yichang Yunhe Park in Hubei province transforms twelve abandoned fish ponds into a green sponge that cleanses polluted canal water. The Yinzhou Central River Transformation in Ningbo restores an urban waterway with wetland planting along its banks. These projects demonstrate how existing urban infrastructure can revive ecological functions. However, the success of such interventions depends on factors such as long-term maintenance, water quality, habitat connectivity, and social impacts on local communities. Understanding cities as shared habitats requires evaluating them not solely by their capacity to protect people, but by the relationships they foster among different life forms.

articles.originalTitle: The Architecture Drawing Prize Announces 11 Recipients for Its 2026 Edition - ArchDaily
articles.title: The Architecture Drawing Prize Announces 11 Recipients for Its 2026 Edition
articles.excerpt: Now in its ninth edition, The Architecture Drawing Prize has announced 11 recipients selected from 168 entries worldwide. The overall recipient will be announced in London in early 2027.
articles.content: Co-curated by Make Architects, Sir John Soane's Museum, and the World Architecture Festival, The Architecture Drawing Prize has announced the 11 recipients of its ninth edition. Selected from 168 entries from around the world, the special prize for hand-drawing was awarded to Ross Cameron for his pencil drawing of scaffolding at the Glasgow School of Art. The recognized works engage with subjects including memory, housing, climate, and myth. Notable entries include Ioana Enache's The People's Palace, Bojana Sićović's Urban Scenography, and Javier García Goicoechea's project. The drawings were evaluated by a professional jury comprising Ken Shuttleworth, Ben Langlands, Nikki Bell, Lily Jencks, Federica Minozzi, Narinder Singh Sagoo, Erin McKellar, and Paul Finch. Selected drawings will be displayed at the World Architecture Festival in Florida from November 18 to 20, 2026. The overall recipient will be announced at Sir John Soane's Museum in London, where an exhibition will run from January 27 to February 28, 2027.

articles.originalTitle: Enthusiasm Remains High as Dubai Design Week and Design Doha Biennale Kick Off - WWD
articles.title: Dubai Design Week and Design Doha Biennial Kick Off
articles.excerpt: Despite regional challenges, Dubai Design Week and the Design Doha Biennial 2026 are launching with participants from over 50 countries, celebrating creativity and regional heritage.
articles.content: Despite regional challenges affecting trade, creative enthusiasm remains strong as Dubai Design Week opens its doors through November 8, featuring participants from over 50 countries. Anchored by the UAE Designer Exhibition under the theme Inherited Futures and curated by architect AlZaina Lootah, the event explores how inherited materials and rituals intersect with contemporary design. Key highlights include a collaboration between Yinka Ilori and Veuve Clicquot, Luke Edward Hall's immersive silverware experience for Buccellati, and workshops hosted by MillerKnoll. Additionally, designer Tristan Auer delivers the opening keynote following his appointment to lead the Burj Al Arab restoration, while Molteni&C inaugurates a new flagship on Jumeirah Beach Road. Opening Thursday, the Design Doha Biennial 2026 presents over 15 exhibitions featuring creators from the MENASA region and beyond. Fromm.Lab showcases 12 projects reinterpreting Arab heritage through contemporary design, and the Design Doha Prize announces winners across categories on November 7 at the Museum of Islamic Art, with an international jury led by India Mahdavi.

articles.originalTitle: Drop-in Design: Your Future City - Victoria and Albert Museum
articles.title: Designing the Future City Workshop at the V&A Museum
articles.excerpt: The Victoria and Albert Museum invites families and children aged 5 and over to design future public buildings using recycled materials in a free workshop.
articles.content: The Victoria and Albert Museum is hosting a hands-on town planning event for children and families in collaboration with architectural designer Jahba Anan and RIBA. At the V&A South Kensington, participants will imagine and redesign how schools, hospitals, libraries, and train stations might look in 2050. Drawing inspiration from the Design 1900–Now galleries, the program allows visitors to examine how design has transformed daily life over the past 125 years. Supported by the Adobe Foundation, attendees will use recycled materials to build mini models of their dream buildings and contribute them to a growing city model over five days. The free drop-in event is suitable for ages 5 and above, with all materials provided on-site. Visitors must ensure children are attended at all times. The venue offers comprehensive accessibility features, including baby-changing facilities, quiet spaces, and ear defenders available upon request from the Learning Centre Desk for families requiring sensory support.

articles.originalTitle: Human Unreadable Act III by Operator - Victoria and Albert Museum
articles.title: Operator Duo Livestreams Act Three of Human Unreadable at the V&A
articles.excerpt: Artist duo Operator brings the final act of their Human Unreadable series, examining human and machine agency, to the Victoria and Albert Museum.
articles.content: The Victoria and Albert Museum is hosting a livestream screening of Act III, the final act of the three-part work Human Unreadable by artist duo Operator, on 22 November 2026. Transmitted live from the Whitney Museum of American Art in New York, the multimedia performance examines negotiations between the body, ambition, and technology. The presentation utilizes 100 dance sequences from the Human Unreadable collection, woven together through scripted dialogue, performance art, lighting, scenic design, and an original score. Broadcast across multiple venues, the transmission features real-time editing from multiple camera perspectives. Commissioned by the Whitney Museum of American Art, the event forms part of the museum's digital art season exploring boundaries between human and machine agency.

articles.originalTitle: Morocco’s Design Renaissance Is Underway - WWD
articles.title: Moroccan Design Sector Revives With New Generation of Creators
articles.excerpt: Moroccan designers and creative entrepreneurs are reclaiming their heritage to secure international recognition and pricing power. According to government data, the country's craft exports are on the rise.
articles.content: A new generation of Moroccan designers and creative entrepreneurs is working to revitalize the country's craft heritage and secure broader international recognition. Government data shows that Morocco's craft exports reached 1.232 billion Moroccan dirhams in 2025, rising from 792 million dirhams in 2019. The United States accounted for 49 percent of these exports, followed by France at 10.5 percent. Organized by Hanane El Moutii, founder of the strategy firm Éclat, the inaugural edition of Morocco Design took place in Casablanca from October 5 to 7. The citywide program featured exhibitions, workshops, and showroom presentations that paired local talent with established international design brands. Industry participants note that while Morocco preserves centuries-old artisan traditions heavily coveted by the global luxury sector, local brands frequently face pricing challenges due to preconceived assumptions about lower production costs. Driven by both domestic talent and returning members of the diaspora, this growing movement aims to shift perceptions and establish long-term prestige for Moroccan creators. Preparations for the 2027 edition are already underway to expand cultural spaces and showcase more local creators.

articles.originalTitle: Marsden Hartley | Painting No. 50 | L1396 - The National Gallery, London
articles.title: Marsden Hartley's Painting No. 50 Reflects His Berlin Years
articles.excerpt: Created in Berlin between 1914 and 1915 by US artist Marsden Hartley, Painting No. 50 blends Native American cultural references with German military pageantry.
articles.content: Painting No. 50, a striking work by US artist Marsden Hartley created as part of his Amerika series after moving to Berlin in 1913, is on display at the National Gallery. Influenced by the militaristic atmosphere of pre-First World War Berlin, the artist integrated the choreography of street parades into his visual vocabulary. At the center of the composition, Hartley stacked simplified elements such as a teepee, a canoe, and a bow and arrow, incorporating black and yellow zigzags reminiscent of military insignia alongside concentric target-like circles. Although he had no direct contact with Native American communities while living in the United States, Hartley drew inspiration from popular culture and ethnographic museum collections in Paris and Berlin. This synthesis allowed him to align with the European avant-garde while simultaneously crafting a distinct American identity for European audiences. Due to wartime travel restrictions and rising hostility toward immigrants, Hartley returned to his home country in 1915. The oil on canvas composition is on loan from the Terra Foundation for American Art and is exhibited in Room 45.

articles.originalTitle: HISTORICAL ARCHIVE | The Pillar and Ground of the Truth by Pavel A. Florenskij - La Biennale di Venezia
articles.title: Venice Biennale Stages Pavel A. Florensky Project at Historical Archive
articles.excerpt: The Historical Archive of La Biennale di Venezia will present a five-day special project dedicated to Pavel A. Florensky, exploring the relationship between language and truth. The performances will take place from 16 to 20 November at the Arsenale.
articles.content: La Biennale di Venezia is presenting The Pillar and Ground of the Truth by Pavel A. Florensky as part of the Biennale of the Word. Taking place from 16 to 20 November 2026 at the new premises of the Historical Archive at the Arsenale, the project is conceived and directed by Antonello Pocetti across five evenings. The texts have been adapted from Florensky's writings to convey the depth of his reflections. Each evening opens with contributions from figures in culture, philosophy, and religion, followed by staged readings. Born in 1882 in Yevlakh, Azerbaijan, Florensky studied mathematics in Moscow before turning to philosophy and theology. Ordained an Orthodox priest in 1911, he engaged in research spanning mathematics, music, painting, and philosophy. Following the 1917 Revolution, he remained in Russia, where he participated in scientific projects before being arrested on counter-revolutionary charges and executed near Leningrad on 8 December 1937. Tickets become available starting 29 October on the La Biennale di Venezia website.

articles.originalTitle: Michele Bönan Has Been Designing Hotels for Over 50 Years. And Is Still at the Top of His Game - WWD
articles.title: Hotel Designer Michele Bönan Discusses His Career and New Projects
articles.excerpt: Having designed over 50 hotels, Florentine architect Michele Bönan noted that the definition of luxury has evolved and announced a new palace project in Naples.
articles.content: Designing hotels for over 50 years, Florentine architect Michele Bönan stated that the definition of luxury in the hospitality sector has changed, with guests increasingly seeking privacy, wellness, and a sense of belonging. Blending Italian craftsmanship with contemporary art and antiques, Bönan has created projects for brands such as Rocco Forte Hotels, the Lungarno Collection, and J.K. Place. Having recently completed the 12 residences of Casa J.K. Place Roma on Via dei Prefetti in Rome, the architect announced he is preparing the Palazzo dei Principi Caravita di Sirignano in Naples, with its cornerstone laid in 1535, to open in 2027. The historic property, long used as an insurance company hub, is slated to be transformed to evoke the feeling of a prince's house. Having launched the Michele Bonan Interiors collection in 2021 with his son Sky Bonan, the designer emphasizes treating every project with the warmth of a home.
